notes.meaning: Jesus and his companions traveled to the village of Cana in Galilee for a wedding feast. Mary, his mother, was already there, likely helping out because the family were relatives or close friends. Wedding celebrations in Jewish culture were joyful community gatherings that often lasted an entire week.

The host invited Jesus along with the small group of disciples who had recently started following him. By attending the feast and sharing in their joy, Jesus showed that he honors marriage and family life. His presence blessed the gathering rather than pulling people away from everyday human celebrations.

The feast ran out of wine, which was an embarrassing social failure for the bridegroom and his family. Mary noticed the shortage and brought the problem straight to Jesus, trusting his goodness and power to help. She placed the quiet need before him, expecting him to act in his own way.

Jesus addressed Mary with the respectful title "Woman," but gently showed that his divine mission is directed by the Father rather than family requests. His "hour"—the appointed time to reveal his glory fully in his death and resurrection—had not yet arrived. He would still help, but only according to God's heavenly timing.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Mary acts as an intercessor whose prayer moves Jesus to begin his public signs, and calling her 'Woman' points to the woman of Genesis who opposes the serpent.

notes.meaning: Mary accepted his reply with humble trust, confident that Jesus would do what was best. She instructed the servants to listen carefully and carry out whatever command he gave them. Her faith pointed people away from herself and completely toward Christ.

Six large stone jars stood nearby, holding water used for the ceremonial hand-washing required by Jewish traditions. Stone vessels were preferred because Jewish customs considered stone less likely than clay to become ritually unclean. Together, the jars held well over a hundred gallons, showing the huge scale of the blessing about to come.

Jesus told the household servants to fill all the empty stone jars completely with plain water. Filling them right to the brim proved that nothing else had been added or mixed in. The obedience of the servants made them firsthand witnesses of the Lord's power.

As soon as the jars were full, Jesus told the servants to dip some out and take it to the man in charge of the feast. It took real faith for the servants to carry what had just been water to the chief official. Without speaking any special words or touching the vessels, Jesus quietly transformed the liquid.

The master of the banquet tasted the liquid and discovered that it was delicious wine. He had no idea what had taken place, which meant his praise of the drink was completely honest and unbiased. Only the servants who had drawn the water knew that a divine miracle had occurred.

The banquet leader noted the common practice of hosts serving their best wine first and bringing out cheaper wine later when tastes were dulled. The wine Jesus created was far superior to what the host had provided at the start. In a deeper sense, Christ brings the rich joy of God's new kingdom to replace old ceremonial washings.

differ.view: Jesus made real fermented wine, showing that drinking wine in moderation is lawful while drunkenness alone is condemned.
Jesus created completely pure, unfermented grape juice, because scripture warns against intoxicating drink and calls believers to total abstinence.

notes.meaning: Turning water into wine was the very first miraculous sign Jesus worked in his public ministry. By this display of creative authority, he revealed his divine glory as the true Son of God. Seeing this sign deepened the faith of his disciples and confirmed that he was indeed the Messiah.

Following the wedding, Jesus traveled down from the hills of Galilee to the lakeside city of Capernaum with his mother, his brothers, and his disciples. This city soon became his main base of ministry in Galilee. They stayed there only a few days because the annual Passover feast in Jerusalem was approaching.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Mary remained a perpetual virgin, so the 'brothers' mentioned here were close kinsmen such as cousins rather than biological children of Mary.

notes.meaning: Passover was the great annual spring festival remembering how God delivered the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. As an obedient Jewish worshiper living under the Law of Moses, Jesus traveled up to Jerusalem to observe the feast at the temple. This trip marks the start of his recorded public work in Judea.

Inside the outer court of the temple, Jesus found a noisy marketplace. Merchants were selling cattle, sheep, and doves for sacrifices, while money changers exchanged foreign currency into the special temple coinage. What had begun as a service for traveling pilgrims had crowded out the court where Gentiles were supposed to pray.

Jesus made a whip out of cords and drove the cattle and sheep out of the sacred grounds. He dumped out the money changers' coins and flipped their tables upside down. A holy awe from God fell upon the area, so that none of the merchants dared to stop him.

Jesus commanded the dove sellers to take their cages and leave the temple grounds immediately. He rebuked them for corrupting the place of worship into a noisy market for worldly gain. By calling the temple "My Father's house," Jesus openly claimed a unique, divine Sonship with God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Jesus cleansed the temple only once at the end of his life, and John placed the event at the start of his Gospel for theological reasons rather than chronological order.

notes.meaning: Watching his bold actions, the disciples remembered the words of Psalm 69:9. The scripture spoke of the Messiah's burning love for the holiness of God's house, a passion so intense that it would consume him. His courage in clearing the temple proved that he was completely devoted to his Father's honor.

The Jewish religious leaders were astonished by his actions and demanded an explanation. Instead of asking whether the market was wrong, they asked for a miracle to prove he had the authority to cleanse the temple. They believed only a recognized prophet or ruler had the right to make such sweeping reforms.

Jesus replied with a riddle, pointing forward to his coming death and resurrection. He stated that if they destroyed this temple, he would raise it back up in three days. His bodily resurrection from the dead would be the final, undeniable proof of his divine authority.

The leaders misunderstood his words and scoffed at what sounded like an absurd claim. They assumed he was talking about Herod's grand stone temple, which had taken forty-six years of ongoing construction and remodeling up to that time. They could not imagine how any single man could rebuild such a massive structure in three days.

John makes clear that Jesus was speaking about his own physical body, not the building in Jerusalem. Just as God dwelt among his people in the temple, the full presence of God lived inside Jesus Christ. When his enemies put him to death, his body would be raised to life again.

The disciples did not understand what Jesus meant when he first spoke these words. Only after he rose from the dead did they remember his statement and grasp its true meaning. This fulfilled promise led them to trust the Old Testament scriptures and Jesus' own teachings even more firmly.

During the week of the Passover festival in Jerusalem, Jesus performed various miraculous signs among the people. Many saw these wonders and believed in his name as a teacher sent by God. Yet much of this belief was shallow, stirred by spectacular miracles rather than genuine, heart-deep repentance.

Even though many people professed to believe in him, Jesus did not entrust his mission or his safety to them. He knew how easily human crowds change from enthusiastic praise to anger and betrayal. He acted with wise caution because he could see through every outward profession.

Jesus never needed anyone to report on what a person was truly like, because he already knew every human heart. As the divine Son of God, he understood the secret motives and hidden thoughts of all people. We can take comfort that our Savior knows us completely, yet still offers us his grace.
